input:
This pricing case examines a contract cleaning service and asks whether the service, as currently priced, is capable of covering its costs. The bottom line is not encouraging: the break-even volume is 6762 units per year, whereas the volume achieved last year was only 5052 units per year, leaving the business short by 1710 units per year.

The service is priced at $129 per unit, while the variable cost amounts to $66 per unit, so each unit sold generates a contribution of $63 per unit towards fixed costs of $426k per year. In practical terms, volume needs to climb to 6762 units per year before the accumulated contribution covers those fixed costs in full. Every additional unit sold above the current 5052 units contributes a further $63 towards closing the gap, whilst the fixed costs remain unchanged across that range. It should be noted that the volume figures are last year's actual results rather than forecasts. Crucially, the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated, and the case gives no indication of what volume might be at any other price. A change in price therefore cannot be evaluated from these figures, since the break-even volume at a new price would rest on an assumed volume response rather than a measured one. In summary, the service either has to sell an extra 1710 units per year at the current price, or revisit the price or the cost base using evidence this case does not contain.
